meta.title: How Does Fox News Frame the WNBA?
meta.description: Analyzing the right-wing politicization of the Women’s National Basketball Association
meta.hed: How Does Fox News Frame the WNBA?
meta.dek: Analyzing the right-wing politicization of the Women’s National Basketball Association
meta.headerImg: wnba-framed.png | The WNBA logo hung inside an empty gilt picture frame

content.value: I’ve loved basketball and played it (mediocrely) all my life, but I only became a WNBA fan when I moved to Seattle five years ago. (Let’s go, Storm!) Since then, I’ve also become fixated on a question: Why is Fox News ((obsessed|tv: cable)) with the WNBA?

fox-iran-wnba.png | Fox News homepage navigation listing its Hot Topics: War With Iran, then WNBA Controversy | A screenshot from the Fox News home page in August 2026. Their hottest topics: literal war and women’s basketball.
The realization dawned on me slowly, especially since I don’t read or watch Fox News myself.

The first clue came at a family gathering while chatting with an older conservative family member. Out of the blue, they started name-dropping WNBA players, praising superstar Caitlin Clark, while making  suspect comments about Black players.
This person has never seen a WNBA game in their life. But they do mainline Fox News on cable TV.
The second clue: my web browser. As I started reading more WNBA news, I was recommended more. That made sense. But then I started getting served coverage from, of all places, Fox News.

Headline after headline pitted the league’s most famous straight white star, Clark, against other WNBA players, mainly Black and/or queer women, like Alyssa Thomas, DiJonai Carrington, or Angel Reese.

clips: June 2026 | pink | Caitlin Clark ((Caitlin Clark|face))  fans ==unload== on WNBA, Alyssa Thomas ((Alyssa Thomas|face)) after ==violent sequence== leaves Fever star battered
January 2025 | green | WNBA star ((DiJonai Carrington|face)) who ==hurt Caitlin Clark's ((Caitlin Clark|face)) eye== calls for league to take action ==against Trump administration policies==
May 2025 | pink | Dave Portnoy calls Angel Reese ((Angel Reese|face)) ==a jacka-- for jealousy of Caitlin Clark== ((Caitlin Clark|face)) in response to ESPN analyst

content.value: When it comes to sports, there are, at least seemingly, facts. This team won, and this team lost. This player scored a lot of points. You would expect a lot of similar coverage. But these headlines were clearly different.
So I decided to collect some data.  How does Fox News cover the WNBA compared to everybody else?

steps.text: Let’s start with article headlines in online coverage. This chart compares Fox News to other outlets: ESPN, CBS Sports, USA Today, The Athletic, and Just Women’s Sports (see methods for how these outlets were chosen). If all outlets mentioned Caitlin Clark equally, she would be in the middle.
But Fox News mentions Clark 3.2x more than other outlets.
steps.clip: race | July 2026 | pink | CNN's Abby Phillip claims GOP lawmakers back ==Caitlin Clark== exclusively because she is White

steps.text: Here’s where the other players stand. Further to the right is more attention from Fox, further to the left is more attention from the other outlets.

steps.names: A’ja Wilson, Napheesa Collier, Breanna Stewart
steps.text: Fox News discusses all-stars like Napheesa Collier, Breanna Stewart, and A’ja Wilson approximately 3-6x less than other outlets…
… and instead gives more coverage to conflict-driven storylines like Sophie Cunningham’s statements about trans athletes,
DiJonai Carrington’s high-profile fouls,
Angel Reese’s animosity toward Clark,
Natasha Cloud’s outspoken activism for BLM, Gaza, and trans rights,
and Brittney Griner’s Russian imprisonment and gender identity.

For years and across topics, Fox News has stoked “hate” and relied on “us vs. them” narratives (e.g., Clark vs. Reese), but that playbook didn’t really extend to the WNBA and its players until more recently.

content.value: The Fox News-WNBA Expanded Universe

Seven years ago, Fox News’ WNBA headlines — like many outlets’ — were few and far between. When they did write about the league, it was for run-of-the-mill events: Cathy Engelbert hired as the commissioner, Sue Bird out with an injury, Napheesa Collier claiming Rookie of the Year honors.

Over time and against a backdrop of Black Lives Matter protests, a second Trump presidency, and a historic CBA, Fox News seized on the expanding league as a culture-war target, framing it as both dangerously radical and illegitimate.
Let’s go back in time to see the evolution.

steps.text: In 2019, there were barely a handful of Fox News headlines about the WNBA each month. Here, each face is someone Fox News named in a WNBA headline and the size is how often they appeared.
Around 2021 Fox News' coverage begins to drift more political, and they start to stage clashes and connections in headlines. Here, a line means two people shared a headline.

steps.focus: Joe Biden, Megan Rapinoe, Sue Bird
steps.text: Fox underscored connections between the players’ 2020 BLM activism and then-President Joe Biden, and between point guard Sue Bird (and her then-girlfriend Megan Rapinoe) and Democrats.
steps.headline: Biden praises WNBA champs for ==social justice activism== | Sue Bird, Megan Rapinoe attempt to dial up ==support for Democrats== before Election Day |

steps.text: They dramatized conflict between Lebron James and Kelly Loeffler, a former WNBA owner and former senator. In 2021, Loeffler was defeated by Democrat Raphael Warnock, in part thanks to WNBA player advocacy.
steps.headline: LeBron James suggests buying WNBA team from Georgia Sen. Kelly Loeffler after projected loss

steps.text: Then in 2022, Brittney Griner became the central WNBA focal point, because she was arrested and imprisoned in Russia. The league was suddenly imbricated with broader world politics.

After Griner was freed in a prisoner swap, Fox notably turned to Donald Trump to suggest it was a bad deal.

He plainly devalued her life—and so did Fox by consistently airing this framing.
steps.headline: Trump: Brittney Griner prisoner swap for 'Merchant of Death'  ==doesn't seem like a very good trade==

steps.text: Clark joined the WNBA in 2024 and fully took the spotlight.
She was often pitted against Reese.

steps.focus: Caitlin Clark, Angel Reese, Dave Portnoy
steps.text: To foster animosity between them, Fox News turned to people like Dave Portnoy (Barstool Sports).
steps.headline: Dave Portnoy calls Angel Reese a =='jacka--' for 'jealousy' of Caitlin Clark== in response to ESPN analyst

steps.text: After Sophie Cunningham was traded and joined Clark (and Lexie Hull) on the Fever, forming the “Tres Leches,” she became the second largest connection in 2026.
At the same time, Fox increasingly platformed anti-trans advocates like Enes Kanter Freedom and Riley Gaines.
This brings us to the summer of 2026 when the right-wing politicization of the WNBA burst into the mainstream.

content.value: In July, Sophie Cunningham ((Sophie Cunningham|face))—Clark’s teammate and on-court “bodyguard”—made anti-trans remarks. While she told ESPN that she “got a lot of negative feedback about me hating trans” and clarified that “I never once said that," she also expressed a desire to “protect young girls in a locker room, or young girls in sport who shouldn't have to go against biological men"—using the exact language and hateful agenda items of the anti-trans movement. She later doubled down on those comments.
This inspired right-wing politicians and anti-trans advocates around the world to rally around her, including Vice President J.D. Vance, J.K. Rowling, and Jennifer Sey.
vance-cunningham-fox.png | Fox News segment showing Vice President J.D. Vance praising Sophie Cunningham | Vice President J.D. Vance praises Sophie Cunningham on Fox News, August 2026.

Trans women’s participation in the WNBA has become a non-stop Fox News talking point. On television, they’ve spent more than 13 hours (!) discussing the WNBA this summer alone. It’s worth repeating: no transgender players are currently in the league.

As Fox News pundit Jesse Watters recently said on air: “We have to do this again, really? Someone wore a t-shirt at a WNBA game? This isn’t a news story…. We don’t even cover the NBA. Why are we covering the WNBA?”
Fightin’ Words
It’s not just the amount of attention that Fox devotes to the WNBA that’s the issue. It’s also the language they use.
To measure this, we’re going to use a method (aptly) called “fightin’ words,” which shows the most distinctive words used by one group vs. another.

steps.text: Here’s how Fox’s vocabulary (right side) differs from other outlets (left side) when reporting on the WNBA. This should look familiar.

steps.words: Caitlin Clark, Sophie Cunningham, Angel Reese, DiJonai Carrington, Breanna Stewart, lynx, liberty, aces
steps.text: You can see Fox’s outsized focus on Clark, Cunningham, Reese, and Carrington, and the relative neglect of players like Stewie (Breanna Stewart) or other leading teams (Aces, Liberty).
When we switch to looking at phrases instead of words, you can see the coverage gap between Fox News and other outlets even more.

steps.words: social media, white privilege, hard foul, biological men, transgender athletes, white house, fever star, points rebounds, free agency
steps.text:
Fox consistently uses culture war phrases and dog whistles, like “white privilege” (derogatory) and “biological men” (derogatory, referring to trans women), and amplifies social media controversies.

Meanwhile, other outlets talk about actual strategy and game play, like points and rebounds or free agency.

content.value: What about language around specific players, like Clark?  ((Caitlin Clark|face))

This is a juicy question because there is currently a “fight over Caitlin Clark’s soul,” as University of Washington professor Kate Starbird, a leading misinformation researcher and former WNBA player, put it to me. With collaborators, she’s currently studying “outrage bait” around the league on social media.

When Clark joined the league in 2024, the WNBA culture war debates really heated up. Some commentators noted that Clark’s background as a straight, white, Midwestern star may play a role in her broad appeal—a point that conservatives and Fox News pundits have rejected.

clark-fever-spurlock.jpg | Caitlin Clark, seen from behind in her white Indiana Fever number 22 jersey, releases a jump shot toward the basket. | Photo by Brian Spurlock/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images
But Clark is not a “stable” figure for the conservative or liberal media, Starbird said. And it’s not totally clear what her legacy will be.

One factor in the mix: social media. Starbird has previously pointed to the growing pressure athletes feel from their large online audiences. “The real risk for internet influencers—a class of celebrities that increasingly includes professional athletes—isn’t ‘falling down rabbit holes,’ but being ‘captured’ and radicalized by their audiences,” Starbird said. Social media dynamics also shape Fox’s coverage. They’re on the hunt for clicks and comments, and they know that subtle hints and coded language can metastasize into bolder claims among regular internet users, provocateurs, and content farms.

The point is that, at least right now, Clark is often talked about more than she talks (at least off the court, and not to the refs). And sometimes the conservative media uses her as a pawn. Let’s take a closer look at the coverage.

content.value: You can see the divergent framing even with specific incidents. When The Athletic wrote about a play-off game where DiJonai Carrington accidentally poked Caitlin Clark in the eye, for example, they opened by minimizing the incident. They emphasized that Clark herself “downplayed” it. It was an accident.

value.caption: Flip through the coverage to see more diverging moments, including Fox’s glowing portrayal of Cunningham’s fouls next to their racist description of Alyssa Thomas’s “thug-like play.”

He appears to be implying… that ==Caitlin Clark receives favorable treatment== because she is a generational talent with a massive fan base and ==because she is white==.

content.value: By contrast, Fox News opened with a dramatic, descriptive scene of Carrington sticking her “long fingernail” into Clark’s eye, burying Clark’s comments about intentionality paragraphs later.

People get completely fixated on this kind of story. Case in point: this summer I was waiting at a bus stop in my Storm gear, headed to watch them play Carrington' s team, the Chicago Sky, when a random man rolled down his truck window and yelled that he hoped there wouldn’t be any dangerous fouls or funny business… Go away, sir.
“Rejecting” Identity Politics

Fox News vociferously rejects “identity politics” in WNBA coverage. They’ve accused outlets like ESPN, USA Today, and The Athletic of being “racial idolaters” and generally injecting left-wing politics about race, gender, and sexuality into their reporting.

everything's-racist-fox.png | Laura Ingraham and Clay Travis, founder of OutKick, discussing Clark on Fox News. | Laura Ingraham and Clay Travis—the founder of OutKick—discuss a USA Today column that suggested some of Clark’s fans were racist.

Here’s the irony: Fox News talks more about race, gender, and identity in the WNBA than any other outlet. They’ve mentioned race or racial politics in 16% of their WNBA articles overall, and 23% this year, more than twice as much as The New York Times, USA Today, and ESPN. Meanwhile, Fox mentioned LGBTQ+ topics in 11% of WNBA articles overall and 34% in 2026, far more than any other outlet.
Does this difference reflect the fact that Fox News writes more opinion-oriented coverage, while the other outlets stick to sports? I don’t think so—at least not entirely.

For one thing, this comparison includes any opinion pieces or cultural reporting from The New York Times and the Athletic, ESPN (including from Andscape), the Washington Post, and USA Today. Yet the editorialized coverage from Fox is telling in its own right. Few (if any) outlets write about the WNBA quite so much from a cultural and political perspective.

content.value: Across many outlets, discussion of race peaked in 2020, when WNBA players engaged in highly visible protest in support of BLM. They walked off the court during the national anthem and wore BLM and “Say Her Name” shirts on national television.

wnba-blm-2020.jpg | Minnesota Lynx players standing with linked arms, wearing “Say Her Name” shirts | Minnesota Lynx players wear “Say Her Name” shirts and link arms in honor of Breonna Taylor before a game in July 2020. Phelan M. Ebenhack/AP
But unlike other outlets, Fox News continued to make race a focal point after 2020, especially in relation to “race baiting” and “race bullies” around Clark.

content.value: Fox’s obsession with race and with the LGBTQ+ community, especially transgender women, are not disconnected. In fact, they’re intimately connected. By dramatizing the danger posed to Clark—and the reverse white racism she supposedly faces—Fox News riles up their base against the broader WNBA, which includes not only many Black women but many gay and queer women, too. According to a recent Atlantic article by Jemele Hill, the league is approximately 70 percent Black, and somewhere between 25 to 35 percent queer.

In a further twist, Fox News often highlights white players who conform to traditional conventions of femininity—like Cunningham, Kelsey Plum, or Cameron Brink—and denigrates Black players who do not, advancing conceptions of ideal (straight white femme) womanhood. Drawing these boundaries has only one obvious end: hating women, including trans women.

value.title: Foul talk inspired Republican threats and set the stage for trans hate
value.subtitle: Fox News’s use of {swatch}hip-check, poke, punch or throat, or {swatch2}“protect” (in articles, per month)
value.sourceNote: An article counts once, however often it uses them.

content.value: One particularly powerful right-wing WNBA narrative—which arguably ties both implicit racism and transphobia together—is about fouls.

From the moment Clark entered the league, conservatives have pushed a story that other players are purposely targeting her on the court, often suggesting because she is white. While Clark has faced real physicality, and there have been demands for improved refereeing across the board, the politicized dimension of this story is pure right-wing spin. This ramped up to the point that in July 2026 a group of Republican politicians literally sent a letter to the WNBA commissioner, threatening to call for an “investigation by the Department of Justice, the Department of Labor, or the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission."
letter-highlighted.jpg | Letter from Republicans to the WNBA commissioner | Letter from Republicans to the WNBA commissioner | small

The Republicans cite, as evidence, the fact that “Clark has been hip-checked, poked in the eye, and struck in the throat during games.” Who emphasized exactly these points for months and months? Fox News. Across more than two hundred articles, Fox mentioned these exact words and phrases, and they often talked about the importance of “protecting” Clark from such dangerous behavior.

Then, in summer 2026, the “protect Caitlin Clark” conversation gave way to the “protect women and children” from transgender players conversation, a framing that has been weaponized against trans women for a long time.

value.title: What about Fox News coverage on TV?
value.teaser: Fox News vs. CNN and MSNBC

content.value: Though Fox News claims that everybody else is talking about racism, they’re the ones talking about it the most, including on TV.

value.note: Cable news chyrons, {period}, from the Internet Archive’s Third Eye.

content.value: 84 percent of the time “racist” appeared in a WNBA chyron on cable news, it was on Fox.

Fouls against Caitlin Clark, especially specific physical contact in specific incidents with Black players, was hammered home on TV, too—so much so that even chyrons, the most condensed breaking news summaries, specifically included these terms.
They also discuss trans women in sports and the WNBA in hundreds of segments.

value.note: Cable news chyrons, {period}, from the Internet Archive’s Third Eye.

content.value: Let’s Not Get Played

This coverage matters. Many Republican politicians, including Trump, regularly consume Fox News and are swayed by it. Fox is also an influential node in a diffuse network of conservative media, including fringe right-wing blogs. According to Open Measures, these blogs published more than 14,000 posts about the WNBA in the last few months, and attracted more than 46,000 comments.
In 2026, Fox discussed the WNBA more than ever, with 27 percent of their online coverage mentioning trans athletes or issues.

content.value: As their own pundit Jesse Watters openly said on air, Fox News ((doesn’t actually care about women’s basketball.|tv: watters)) Right-wing agitators are using the WNBA to push their own agendas. Fox News is exploiting these phenomenal athletes as lucrative ragebait.
And it’s working. In August 2026, Fox’s OutKick had 13 million visitors, the most in its history.
The problem is not that women’s basketball is being made political. ((Sports are, and have always been, political.|tv: kaepernick))

The problem is that these narratives are so fabricated from the outside and so at odds with the actual politics of most WNBA players. In fact, Roxane Gay recently argued that the league should step up and match its players’ ((historic activism|tv: sayhername)), that they “should lead the charge for making space for trans women in women’s sports” and shield their players “from bad-faith attacks, death threats, harassment and other racial animus.”
This would certainly be consistent with the league’s spirit. When I went to my first WNBA game, I was shocked by how inclusive it felt.
Black, queer, and POC women were celebrated ((on the court.|tv: mcbride))
And ((off the court.|tv: pride))
The dancers were teenaged girls doing ((sick hip-hop moves|tv: dancers))  in baggy pants.
The Storm’s adorably goofy mascot, ((Doppler|tv: doppler)) , uses they/them pronouns.
The whole vibe is truly ((so nice and welcoming.|tv: kiss))
And the basketball is ((electric.|tv: arike))

I don’t know how the WNBA will handle all of this increased attention—from the media, politicians, activists, trolls, new fans, and (unfortunately) my conservative relatives. But I know one thing for sure. The ragebait version of the WNBA is not recognizable to me.
We need to see this framing for what it is, and push back against it, lest we all get played.

Data & Methods

Headlines and Articles. I collected any Fox News article (both headline and full text) that mentioned the WNBA or its players from 2019-2026. This corpus includes coverage from Outkick, now owned by Fox and published on their site.

value.caption: 2019–2026. Fox News includes OutKick; ESPN includes Andscape; CBS includes CBS Sports and CBS News; the New York Times includes The Athletic.

content.value: As a comparison, I collected parallel WNBA coverage from ESPN, USA Today, CBS Sports, The Athletic (owned by the New York Times), and Just Women’s Sports.

TV Chyrons. I gathered nine years worth of cable news chyrons from Fox, MSNBC, and CNN, drawing on data from the Internet Archive's Third Eye OCR feed, and inspired by a very cool analysis by Charlie Smart.

Players. In this analysis, I include the 30 WNBA players named most in Fox News articles. For the network, I consider individuals named in 10 or more headlines, and add specific politicized individuals like J.D. Vance, Michelle Obama, and Charlie Kirk.
Fightin Words. The word comparisons use “fightin’ words” aka weighted log-odds with an informative Dirichlet prior (Monroe, Colaresi & Quinn 2008).
You can find data and code on GitHub.
